title: Live: Trump prime-time address expected to cover election denial claims
description: US President Donald Trump is set to give a prime-time national address about newly declassified intelligence on investigations into elections. Follow live.
content_snippet: Good morning. US President Donald Trump says he has "really, really big news", and he's about to give a prime-time national address to tell the world. What's it about, you might be asking? While w…
author: Elissa Fitzgerald
full_text: Donald Trump claims China acquired personal information of 220 million US voters — as it happened Live updates Recap Here is a summary of the day's events: - US President Donald Trump has declassified documents that he says contain evidence China has interfered with US elections since 2018. - In a national address, he claimed China acquired the personal information and voting data of 220 million Americans, which it used to manipulate public opinion against him. - Ahead of his speech, Democrats suggested the president would use claims of interference to justify seizing unconstitutional control over elections from states. New: Filters Choose what information you see below by using filters Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 4:00pm That's all for now! Thank you for sticking with us through what has been a big day of live coverage, picking apart US President Donald Trump's extraordinary prime-time speech regarding his administration's allegations that China sought to influence American voters. We'll be ending our blog here but if you're looking to dive a little deeper into today's developments, my Washington DC-based ABC colleague Brad Ryan has everything you need in the article linked just below. And, as always, you can find even more of our reporting on this issue and much more via the ABC News website and mobile app. Until next time, have a great evening! Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 3:50pm Solomon says he's seen no intelligence that votes were flipped Conservative commentator John Solomon, who joined the White House staff last month as a special government employee, was seated in the East Room for US President Donald Trump's speech. He later told MS NOW that "the intelligence community has zero evidence that someone has flipped — that a foreign power flipped — a vote in 2020, 22 or 24." "We're not through all the documents," he added. Asked whether the 2020 election results were still accurate, Solomon said he was "still researching". — with AP Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 3:45pm Trump-picked officials clashed with US intelligence assessment of China election influence, emails show A significant clash of opinions regarding the framing of the true extent of China's influence on the 2020 US election has become apparent among documents included in today's intelligence. On July 1, 2020 a CIA World Intelligence Review (WIRe) memo was released internally among US government agencies that said: "China is probing the presidential campaign for opportunities to tailor collection and gather insight on policy positions on US-Chinese issues." The document claimed "Chinese cyber actors" had targeted the email accounts of high-level US officials since 2017. But according to today's intelligence documents, the US Intelligence Community (IC) — which includes 18 federal agencies such as the CIA and the National Security Agency (NSA) — in 2020 declared that "China does not currently intend to covertly interfere to try to sway the outcome of the election". The declassified intelligence shows that sparked a flurry of internal government agency emails sent by president-picked officials between September 2020 and the end of 2021 questioning the framing of that IC assessment. On September 3, 2020, an officer working for the Director of National Intelligence wrote in an email: "I am concerned about politics seeping into this. There's no reason we can't say that we have [redacted] confidence, etc." On November 20, 2020, an intelligence analyst with the NSA wrote in an email: "We have deliberately massaged our one pending [Presidential Daily Briefing] to avoid any direct links to the election." On the same day, an unnamed Election Threat Analysis Director with the National Intelligence Council responded: "[The NSA's] PDB isn't going to tie to the election? The mind boggles". Two months earlier, that same director wrote: "Is it just me, or are they basically saying we should self-censor our assessment on preference because it could be misused?" Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 3:35pm How have voting advocates reacted? Voting rights advocates and election experts have largely panned the president's speech. Election law expert Rick Hansen said it was "underwhelming", and said the revelations failed to establish that any illegal vote was actually cast, or any election system compromised. "Overall, this was an underwhelming announcement delivered with low energy that changes nothing about how state and local election administrators should run elections," Hansen wrote. New York University's Brennan Center for Justice, an independent and nonpartisan law and policy organisation, said the president was "running out of plays" to gain control over elections. "He has resorted to rehashing old tropes and nothingburgers," a Bluesky post read. "The only way his administration's campaign to undermine our elections works is if voters stay home this fall." Key Event Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 3:27pm Which US states does the White House claim were targeted by China? Earlier we shared with you that among the declassified intelligence documents released today there are claims that China conducted detailed analysis of US voter registration data from at least 18 states. As we were digging through the documents, we uncovered eight of the states that were named as being impacted leading up to the 2020 US election: - Alaska - Connecticut - Florida - Maryland - New York - Washington DC - North Carolina - Kansas We've since continued combing through more of the documents and can now tell you we've found a list of 16 of the 18 impacted states. The other jurisdictions the Trump administration claims China targeted were: Arkansas, Colorado, Georgia, Iowa, Michigan, Ohio, Oklahoma and Rhode Island. A statement from the White House Task Force for Government Transparency says that not all 18 states were identified by name — which is why our list here only includes 16 states. Documents in today's intelligence also claim China's alleged involvement in accessing and analysing personal, identifiable information of US voters extended beyond 2020 and into both 2023 and 2024 — ahead of the last presidential election. Key Event Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 3:23pm Trump cabinet staff will brief state leaders on potential voting safety issues During his address today, Donald Trump suggested it would not be long before action gets underway within his government in a bid to keep election systems secure. The US president said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin would hold a briefing with leaders of states across the country to talk about his department’s cybersecurity findings related to electronic voting systems. Trump described the US's electoral systems as being in “bad shape in so many states” and said his administration was informing political leaders of potential issues in their states. Election experts have long acknowledged the technology used to facilitate elections carries risks that officials work to identify and address. Nationwide, the vast majority of ballots cast included a paper record, helping to prevent cyberattacks or errors from affecting the accuracy of the vote count. Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 3:18pm What to expect at the midterms Several reactions today have speculated that US President Donald Trump is laying the groundwork to dispute the results of the midterm elections scheduled for November 3. The midterms decide the make-up of the House of Representatives and a third of the Senate. That's a a big deal for the president, as it will decide how much power he has to get laws passed. Even now, he is struggling to push unpopular legislation through Congress, and that's expected to get a lot harder after Americans have gone to the polls. The party of the sitting president tends to lose seats at midterm elections. It means Republicans stand to lose control of the House of Representatives (which they currently hold on a very fine margin), and possibly even the Senate. Trump has tried to insulate against this by urging Republican state governments to change their electoral maps to give their party advantages — a practice known as gerrymandering. Some Democratic leaders, particularly in California, fought back by making similar changes in their favour. While the GOP has so far gained a slight edge in this tug of war, it's not yet clear whether it will make enough difference in who ends up in control of Congress by the end of the year. I've taken closer looks at the gerrymandering arms race a few times since it started. Here's one of those stories, which lays out how gerrymandering works in more detail. Key Event Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 3:12pm Trump will order FBI to reopen election fraud investigation in Michigan During his address today, Donald Trump revived a long-debunked claim that election fraud was discovered in the strongly Democratic city of Muskegon, Michigan, involving a large-scale voter registration operation. In the lead-up to the 2020 presidential election, a police raid recovered a batch of voter registration applications collected by a Tennessee-based voter registration company. A review of those applications determined some were legitimate, while others were fraudulent or highly suspicious because of forged signatures, incorrect addresses or other errors. The registrations that were deemed fraudulent were voided before the day of the election and no illegitimate vote linked to any of the applications was cast. But it's still a sticking point for the US president. In 2021, Michigan authorities turned the case over to the FBI — but no-one was ever charged. Today, Trump said he would authorise FBI Director Kash Patel to reopen the investigation into what happened in Michigan. Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson criticised Trump for the move, saying in a statement he "chose to rehash long-debunked and baseless conspiracy theories". Reporting with Reuters Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 2:55pm AP review found there was too little voter fraud to tip the 2020 election An Associated Press review in 2021 dug into every potential case of voter fraud in the six battleground states that US President Donald Trump disputed. It found fewer than 475 cases — a number that would have made no difference in that race. Allegations from Trump of massive voting fraud have been refuted by a variety of judges, state election officials and an arm of his own administration's Homeland Security Department. In 2020, then-Attorney General William Barr, a Trump appointee, said no proof of widespread voter fraud had been uncovered. "To date, we have not seen fraud on a scale that could have effected a different outcome in the election," he said at the time. — with AP Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 2:45pm How many people are registered to vote in the US? During his address, US President Donald Trump said the "voter files" of more than 220 million Americans were acquired by China. A few of you, our readers, have rightfully pointed out in the comments that according to the US Census Bureau, only 174 million Americans are registered to vote (about 73 per cent of the citizen voting-age population). The Trump administration does claim it found thousands of instances of non-citizens enrolled to vote, but this wouldn't account for an almost 50-million disparity. Similarly, the US has recorded about 3 million deaths per year since the pandemic, but even if every one of those people were registered voters, it still wouldn't account for the gap. Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 2:31pm Decentralised elections are more secure It may make the electoral system extraordinarily complicated, but one of the strongest security features of US elections is the fact they aren't conducted at the federal level. America votes in more than 10,000 different election jurisdictions, each with different rules set by state and sometimes local governments. Election security experts say that structure makes the nation's elections safe from widespread fraud. And in the rare instances when misconduct does happen, security protocols frequently catch it. That's because to pull off stealing a presidential election (as Trump claims was done to him in 2020) it would require large numbers of election workers in the most competitive counties across the country who are willing to risk prosecution, prison time and fines while working with officials from both parties willing to look the other way. And everyone somehow would have to keep quiet — a highly unlikely scenario. There are also shared practices and security measures in place across the country that together work to ensure that only eligible voters can cast a ballot and only one ballot is counted for each. — with AP Key Event Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 2:14pm House Democrat says Trump address is pretext to dispute midterm results Represenative Joseph Morelle says he is troubled by the president's apparent attempts to sow confusion and spread misinformation ahead of the midterm elections in November. The New York representative is the ranking Democrat on the House Administration committee, which oversees federal voting and election matters. "This is a pretext for the president, I think, calling into dispute the 2026 elections," Morelle said on C-SPAN. "We have secure elections," he added. "This is a fundamental effort to weaken the foundation of our democracy." Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 1:59pm 'China made thousands of fake driver IDs to send to pro-Beijing students, expats in the US': Preliminary 2020 FBI report Among the declassified intelligence released by the White House today is a series of documents that provide some insight into how US authorities shaped their view of what China was believed to have been doing with regard to American elections. In one information report dated August 2020 and sent to Chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee Chuck Grassley, a Republican senator, the FBI claimed the Chinese government created "a large amount of fraudulent United States drivers licenses" and sent them to the US. "The fraudulent drivers licenses would allow tens of thousands of Chinese students and immigrants sympathetic to the Chinese Communist Party to vote for US Presidential Candidate … Joe [Biden], despite not being eligible to vote in the United States," the report says. "China had collected private US user data from millions of TikTok accounts, to include name, ID and address, which would allow the Chinese government to use real US persons' information to create the fraudulent drivers license. "The fraudulent drivers licenses were to include true ID number and true address of US citizens, making them difficult to detect." The report claimed the people who received the licences in the US would then use them to lodge thousands of mail-in votes. It cited "a collaborative source with indirect access, none of whose reporting has been corroborated for less than one year" as the informant who provided the detail. It's also worth pointing out that this document also explicitly states that it is solely an "information report, not finally evaluated intelligence", meaning it had not been completely analysed and verified by intelligence authorities at the time. Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 1:45pm Analysis: Will this impact the China-America relationship? It was just a few months ago that a gushing US President Trump travelled here to Beijing for a highly anticipated meeting with China's President Xi Jinping. At the time, Mr Trump lavished praise on his Chinese counterpart, calling him a "great leader" and "very smart". The pair shook hands, posed for photos, and enjoyed a lavish state banquet honouring Mr Trump's rare visit. At the time, both leaders hailed the summit as an attempt to stabilise what had been a tumultuous relationship between the world's biggest economic and geopolitical superpowers. But today's speech just goes to highlight how volatile the dynamic remains between America and China. Although Donald Trump's accusations of China meddling in US elections aren't new — and have been debunked through several intelligence investigations — the president's rhetoric runs the risk of inflaming tensions and unsettling diplomatic attempts to steady the US-Sino relationship. China, as it has done in the past, will deny the claims made by Donald Trump. And it's guaranteed there will be state media commentary reinforcing China's position and protesting the accusations. But Mr Xi is expected to visit the United States in September, at the invitation of Mr Trump. While I think it's unlikely Mr Xi would cancel the trip to the US, I also wouldn't be surprised if China used a diplomatic boycott to send a message to America. Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 1:35pm Chinese efforts to collect voter data have long been known Claims that China has gathered data on US voters are not new. A 2020 report by the National Intelligence Officer for Cyber, which was partially declassified in 2022, found that Chinese intelligence officials examined voter registration data from several US states as part of efforts to conduct "public opinion analysis". However, US intelligence agencies did not conclude that Chinese actors directly accessed election systems or manipulated voter records. A joint US government assessment of the 2022 midterm elections also found that suspected Chinese-linked actors collected publicly available voter information. The report stated there was no evidence that these activities interfered with voting. "We have no evidence that any detected activity prevented voting, changed votes, or disrupted the ability to tally votes or to transmit election results in a timely manner; altered any technical aspect of the voting process; or otherwise compromised the integrity of voter registration information or any ballots cast during 2022 federal elections," the report read. Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 1:25pm Where can I read the files? Have the referred to documents actually been released yet? Nothing on the Whitehouse site yet it seems. - Paul Arden Hi Paul, You can find the files on the White House website here. We currently have journalists combing through them, so we'll let you know what we find. My colleague Luke Cooper has shared some of his findings here. Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 1:15pm So where is the SAVE bill at in Congress? While Republican politicians are supportive of the bill, it's not so simple to get it passed. The House of Representatives has already approved the bill, but it stalled in the Senate because of a filibuster. In March, Trump resorted to threatening not to sign any other legislation into law until Congress passed it, but that didn’t clinch him the workaround he hoped. Just this week, senators again tried to resurrect the act by tacking it onto a spending bill for the Department of State and related agencies. Chuck Schumer, the chamber’s top Democrat, has vowed to again block the measure. "I'll say it as many times as it takes: the [SAVE] Act is dead on arrival here in the Senate," Schumer said ahead of the House vote on the spending bill. "I don't care how Republicans try to package their plan to resurrect the old ghost of Jim Crow, we will kill it." If Democrats take the filibuster route, Republicans will need 60 senators in the 100-member chamber to vote to eliminate it. The party has a 53-47 edge in the chamber, but even then, four of those Republicans have indicated they are opposed to the SAVE Act. All of this is to say, it's believed the bill is effectively dead in the water. Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 1:02pm Republicans could gain an electoral edge from the SAVE Act Donald Trump told House Republicans during their annual retreat at his golf club in Florida this year that he doesn't think they will win elections unless voting laws are toughened up. "It'll guarantee the midterms," he said. "If you don't get it, big trouble." He links this to his unfounded claims that election fraud is widespread and cost him an election. But it's also likely to give Republicans a disproportionate advantage. I mentioned earlier today that there's a long-held belief in the US that low overall voter turnout benefits the Republican Party. That's because, even at elections when not many people vote, Republicans consistently turn out at substantially higher rates and that wins them elections. On the flip side, Democratic strategists will tell you that higher voter turnouts will benefit their party. Let's take a look at the 2024 presidential election as an example. Modelling by the data-driven political science publication On Data and Democracy suggests about double the number of Democrats stayed home, compared with Republicans. Voters with a registered party affiliation don’t necessarily always vote in that direction, but it’s a fairly good indicator of what Democrats could stand to gain with higher turnouts, or what Republicans stand to lose. Adding obstacles to the voting process (known as voter suppression) could supercharge that pattern. Other measures that have discouraged voter turnout in recent years include limitations on early and absentee voting, increased queue lengths, and making it a misdemeanour offence to hand out food and drinks to voters waiting in line. That last one was the subject of an episode of Larry David’s Curb Your Enthusiasm. — with AP Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 12:54pm Why is the SAVE Act controversial? Now that we've reached the end of the US President Donald Trump's address, let's delve a bit deeper into the SAVE Act. As I mentioned before, it purportedly aims to block non-citizens from voting, despite that already being an exceedingly rare and isolated occurrence. If it is passed, American citizens would need to show documents like a passport or birth certificate to register to vote, and photo ID to cast votes. So why are voting rights groups and Democrats opposed? It would make it harder for millions of Americans to vote. This would disenfranchise Americans of all ages and races, but in particular, voters of colour (who traditionally lean Democratic) and even people who have married and taken their partner’s name. Research by New York University’s Brennan Center for Justice suggests more than 21 million Americans lack access to these documents. About half of Americans do not have a passport. The act also encroaches on the powers of the states, who, under the Constitution, are in charge of election ballots and procedures. Democrats largely oppose Trump’s efforts to seize more control over elections, and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer said the president’s demands would gridlock the chamber. "This is what he does — he's a thug, he's a bully," he has said. Even Republicans have mixed feelings about the bill, with four senators having declared their opposition: Lisa Murkowski, Susan Collins, Mitch McConnell and Thom Tillis. — with AP Fri 17 Jul 2026 at 12:44pm China 'analysed voter data from 18 US states', declassified memo claims China conducted detailed analysis of US voter registration data from at least 18 states, according to a memo included in the declassified intelligence released by the White House today. The heavily redacted memo claims the Chinese government obtained the voter data from US midterm elections and analysed "personal identifiable information" that could be used to "analyze, discover [redacted] the identities of important U.S. targets". The memo did not detail which year the affected midterm elections were held. The document also claims the data was used to assess public opinion among US voters regarding the country's general elections. While the document claims 18 US states were impacted, only Alaska, Connecticut, Florida, Maryland, New York, Washington DC, North Carolina and Kansas were named. Voter names, birth dates, home addresses, political party affiliations, voter ballot and polling histories, election donation details, military affiliations and some telephone information were included in the data breach, the memo claims. In North Carolina, more than eight million voters were affected by the breach, while information detailing US citizens' occupations and education background was "a priority", the document claims.
